rationale: Matthew 11:27 states a two-way knowledge between Father and Son: "No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son" (BSB). John 10:15 states the same pairing in a different setting and different words: "just as the Father knows Me and I know the Father." Neither text quotes the other, and they belong to different scenes (a prayer after the woes, a shepherd discourse). That is why the type is doctrinal synthesis, two independent statements converging on one claim, and not parallel or quotation. Barnes, read via Bible Hub, makes the link directly: "The same doctrine is clearly taught often in the New Testament. See John 3:35; John 6:46; John 10:15." Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Poole also pair 11:27's "All things" with John 3:35 ("has placed all things in His hands"). The label is strong because the reciprocal wording can be checked in both texts and named commentators connect them. It is not explicit, because neither Gospel refers to the other.
